prime.problem: A two-hour lecture watched straight through feels clear and leaves almost nothing you can rebuild. Without a routine that forces you to build, check and recall, you finish the series able to recognise the code but not write it.
prime.fits: This is the first card of the series. Every later card has the same parts (Prime, Predict first, ▶ Build it, the Study panel), and this card says what each one is for and the order to use them in. The reasons behind that order are in the learning-principles card.
expect: the five-step loop for each lecture
the Study panel, or /study in Claude Code
the note-taking rule: smallest note + "why this matters"
prime.goal: Run the loop on a lecture without looking it up, and say what each step protects you from.

attend: Why does the loop put the big-ideas card before the video rather than after it?
What does a mismatch with "You should see" tell you that a match doesn't, and what should you do before watching on?
Which parts of a card are meant to be done with the card closed, and why closed?
What goes in your notes, what goes in your repo, and what goes nowhere?

must: Priming with the big-ideas card gives each detail a hook → details from the video attach to one of a few claims → you remember the structure, not a pile of steps
Pausing at each ▶ Build it and comparing with a measured output → an error shows up one step after you make it → you debug one small step, not a finished notebook
Study steps done from memory (compress, retrieve, predict) → recalling is harder than recognising → the effort shows exactly what you can't yet explain → you reread only that part
Notes limited to relationships plus "why this matters" → you have to decide what matters as you write → that deciding is the learning, while transcribing puts it off
elevated: Every "You should see" was measured on an M3 with torch 2.14 and a fixed seed → on the same setup a mismatch is your bug, not noise → so build the same environment first (setup card)
reference: the list of card parts in order

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: from memory, draw the five-step loop for one lecture as boxes and arrows, including what happens when your output doesn't match. Next to each step, write one line saying what failure it prevents.
checklist: prime (big-ideas card) → watch + build → Study panel → checkpoints → done when, then the next lecture
the mismatch branch: diff against the lab before watching on
prime prevents unhooked details; build-and-compare prevents late, far-away bugs
the Study panel and checkpoints prevent recognition passing for recall; done when stops you moving on too early
the note rule: smallest note + why this matters, no transcription

retrieve.q: Explain to a friend why this course asks you to type code rather than paste it, when the pasted code would run just the same.
answer: typing forces you to read each line and make each small decision
a typo or a misunderstanding becomes a visible mismatch at that step
pasting gets you a working program without the understanding the course is for

retrieve.q: Walk through what you do from the moment the video reaches a card's timestamp until you press play again.
answer: pause at the ▶ Build it's When
type the code (Karpathy's names), run it
compare with You should see; if it differs, diff against the card's Lab and fix it
check the Done when condition, then resume

retrieve.q: You have 30 minutes left in a session and one card's Study panel not done. Do the panel or start the next chapter of the video? Defend the choice.
answer: do the panel: retrieval right after learning shows the gaps while they're small
the next chapter builds on this card, so gaps compound
starting a new chapter with no time to build it would mean watching without building, which the loop rules out

compare.q: The learning-principles card gives nine study stages; this card gives a five-step loop for each lecture. How do they fit together, and which principle does the ▶ Build it box put into practice?
answer: the five steps are the course-level routine; the nine stages run inside step 3 for each card
Build it puts apply and gap-finding into practice: a real output that either matches or shows where you're wrong
priming is the same idea at both levels: the big-ideas card for the lecture, the Prime block for the card

compare.q: The big-ideas card is used twice in the loop: before the lecture and again at the end. What is it for each time, and how does using it only once fail?
answer: before: priming, reading the claims for the gist without studying them
after: redraw each panel from memory as a retrieval check
only before: no check that you learned it; only after: no hooks while watching

predict.q: You follow the loop for micrograd, and at the += card your a.grad for b = a + a prints 1.0 instead of the card's 2.0. Before looking at your code: which line do you expect is wrong, and what should you not do next?
predict.answer: A _backward closure that uses = instead of +=. The two paths into a each send 1.0, and = keeps only the last one. What not to do is watch on and hope the lecture fixes it. This mismatch is exactly the bug that card is about, and diffing against the lab finds it in one line.

apply.task: Plan your first real session with the loop. Pick micrograd: open its big-ideas card and prime for a few minutes. Then find the first ▶ Build it in the course (the derivative-as-nudge card) and do it at its timestamp. Write a single note in the rule's format.
apply.done: Your f(3.0) prints 20.0 and your slope with h = 0.001 prints about 14.003 (the card's measured value is 14.003000), and your note is one line with a "why this matters".
apply.hint: f(x) = 3x² − 4x + 5. The slope is (f(3 + h) − f(3)) / h.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: where the watch-straight-through plan breaks, or what to do on a mismatch?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why recalling beats rereading, or why typing beats pasting?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: build-and-compare → small bugs, or retrieve → finding gaps?
Which step of the loop are you most likely to skip when you're tired, and what will you do instead?
